summary:
Tonga's Criminal Offences Act criminalises same-sex activity, with a maximum penalty of 10 years' imprisonment. Outright International's overview, updated in March 2026, records no evidence of enforcement in recent years, and the 2010 US State Department human rights report described enforcement as rare.

The same statute contains an offence aimed squarely at gender expression: a male who solicits in public "for an immoral purpose" with intent to deceive as to his true sex commits an offence. This is a trans-expression provision on the books, and unlike the sodomy provision it turns on visible presentation rather than private conduct, so it bears directly on how a trans visitor may appear and speak in public spaces.

Tonga provides no legal gender recognition. A visitor's documents will therefore carry the sex marker assigned at birth, with no domestic mechanism to alter them.

Enforcement of the sodomy provision has been rare or absent in the periods covered by the sources, spanning 2010 to 2026. No documented recent prosecution of a trans person under the solicitation offence appears in the material reviewed.

On protection machinery, the 2010 US State Department report found no reports of government abuses of LGBT persons, while identifying domestic violence, discrimination against women and corruption as the country's most prevalent human-rights problems. That combination points to weak general institutional protection rather than active state persecution.

Tonga has a visible trans-feminine community, known locally as leiti, with a well-known pageant covered by the Washington Post in August 2024 alongside reporting on LGBT rights. Public visibility of leiti people coexists with the criminal statutes rather than being absent from them.

Community infrastructure is thin. Tonga's only LGBTI drop-in centre and shelter, on Tongatapu in Nuku'alofa, had part of its roof torn off by Cyclone Gita in February 2018, with winds over 120 mph damaging the bathrooms and bedrooms used by LGBTI Tongans. The country's sole dedicated shelter facility has documented structural vulnerability.
tangentialFactors:
The gap between legal text and social practice is the defining feature of the risk picture. A statute that criminalises public presentation as deception sits alongside a public, pageanted leiti culture, so legal exposure and social acceptance run on separate tracks and neither predicts the other.

The 2010 US State Department reporting places Tonga's LGBT situation inside a broader pattern of institutional weakness: domestic violence, discrimination against women and corruption were named as the most prevalent problems. Visitors relying on police or administrative remedy should weigh that general environment, not only the specific statutes.

The 2018 cyclone damage to the Nuku'alofa shelter indicates that community safety infrastructure in Tonga is exposed to natural hazard disruption, a factor distinct from legal risk but relevant to anyone seeking support on the ground.

Compared with jurisdictions that have repealed such provisions, Tonga retains both a conduct-based offence and a presentation-based offence, while offering none of the mitigation that legal gender recognition would provide for documents.
localsOnly:
Residents have no route to legal gender recognition, so identity documents, employment records and official interactions remain tied to the sex assigned at birth.

The leiti community maintains established family and church-adjacent social networks and an annual pageant with international coverage, giving trans-feminine Tongans a recognised public presence despite the criminal statutes.

The LGBTI drop-in centre and shelter in Nuku'alofa functions as the country's principal dedicated community facility; its 2018 storm damage affected the bathrooms and bedrooms used by LGBTI Tongans and illustrates the limited redundancy in local support infrastructure.

Prosecution of the sodomy offence has been rare or absent in recent years, according to reporting current to 2026, and no recent prosecution under the public solicitation provision is documented in the sources reviewed.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether corporal punishment remains a statutory penalty under the Criminal Offences Act is unresolved in the sources reviewed; only the 10-year maximum for sodomy is sourced here.

No case records were available establishing how, or whether, the public solicitation offence with intent to deceive as to true sex has been charged or prosecuted. Its enforcement risk is inferred from the text of the statute, not from documented arrests.

The precise scope of "for an immoral purpose" and "true sex" as judicially or administratively interpreted is not sourced, so the practical boundary of the offence for a trans visitor remains open.

UK foreign travel advice for Tonga yielded no trans-specific finding in the material reviewed, leaving that channel without usable content rather than confirming an absence of risk.

Whether any administrative or policy-level route to changing gender markers exists outside formal legal recognition is not addressed by the sources.
